10978-hidden-creek:
Katharine Newlin Burt wrote this 1920 novel about Sheila Arundel, daughter of an artist, Marcus Arundel, who dies at the book's opening. Sheila holds her father's hand through his last night, candlelight falling on their two hands, and inherits both his art world and its troubles. Sylvester Hudson comes for his picture, and the story moves from city studios to a mountain creek.

Part two, The Stars, follows Sheila through loneliness, work, song, winter, and a pack of troubles, toward a quieter life among hills. Burt writes about artists, faith, and the pull of wild country, with a forest fire and a reading of Rossetti's Blessed Damozel marking turning points. The novel blends romance with reflections on art and the natural world.
15704-far-to-seek:
A romance of England and India by Maud Diver, issued by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Diver, known for tales of Anglo-Indian life, dedicates the book as an idyll of a mother and son. Tagore and Fletcher supply epigraphs on longing and endeavour. The novel moves between English homes and Indian stations, following hearts pulled far from home.

A son seeks a distant life while his mother watches, loves, and waits. India offers colour, duty, and danger, while England offers roots and restraint. Diver writes with warmth for both worlds, praising courage without hiding cost. The book appeals to readers who like a long, tender romance where place itself becomes a character.
15875-the-unseen-bridegroom-or-wedded-fo:
A sensational romance by May Agnes Fleming, a popular writer of mystery and love. The tale opens at Mrs. Walraven's ball, on a dark, wet, windy November afternoon in New York. Fifth Avenue gathers in glory for one of the season's most brilliant affairs, though streets run sloppy and sodden outside. Fleming writes for readers who loved secrets, balls, and sudden turns.

A young heroine is wedded for a week to a bridegroom she never sees, in a bargain full of mystery. Love, danger, and hidden identity drive the plot through ballrooms and dark streets. Fleming keeps the pace swift and the feelings high. The novel delights as Victorian sensation fiction: a strange wedding, a veiled husband, and a week that changes a life.
23762-blessed-are-the-meek:
G. C. Edmondson published Blessed Are the Meek in Astounding in September 1955. Its epigraph states its theme: every strength is a weakness, and every weakness is a strength. When the strong start smashing each other's strength, the weak may turn out to be the wise.

Strangers land just before dawn, burning bottom land as they come, and their machines dig up the topsoil. The Old One, in saffron robes, walks down to meet them while Griffin and the linguist Kung Su argue over how to talk to him. The story asks what happens when a powerful, confident expedition meets people it takes for simple folk.
24267-picked-up-at-sea-the-gold-miners-o:
John Conroy Hutcheson wrote this sea and gold-mining adventure, opening aboard the Susan Jane. A piece of floating wreckage brings a boy of fifteen or so aboard, badly injured, struck dumb, and unaware of what passes around him. When Seth is endangered, the boy rushes to help him. In America, while the ship refits, part of the crew, the passenger Mr. Rawlings, and the boy, now called Sailor Bill, go to work a mine Rawlings has bought.

After many adventures, the boy recovers his senses and finds old family friends in the camp: a man and a dog. The mine proves successful, and all go home wealthy. Three shorter nautical tales follow the first in this edition. Readers get a hearty Victorian adventure of sea, mine, and a lost boy found.
24313-once-a-week:
A. A. Milne, author of The Day's Play and The Holiday Round, wrote this book of light pieces. Methuen and Company published it in London, first on October 15, 1914, and in a third edition in 1922. The contents show Milne's range: The Heir, Winter Sport, A Baker's Dozen, A Tragedy in Little, The Financier, The Double, A Breath of Life, Under Entirely New Management, and A Farewell Tour.

Later pieces include The Truth about Home Rails, The King's Sons, Disappointment, and Among the Animals. A Tragedy of the Sea, Old Friends, Getting Married, and Home Affairs follow. An Insurance Act, Bachelor Relics, Lords Temporal, The Missing Card, and Silver Linings close the set. Milne dedicates the book to the collaborator who buys ink and paper and laughs. Readers get urbane, funny essays from the future creator of Winnie-the-Pooh.
25642-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris writes the Greek volume, tenth in his fifteen-volume Historical Tales, subtitled The Romance of Reality, published by Lippincott in Philadelphia and London in 1896. A Greek shepherd at Olympia fronts the book.

How Troy was taken opens the tales, followed by the voyage of the Argonauts, Theseus and Ariadne, and the seven against Thebes. Lycurgus and the Spartan laws, Aristomenes the hero of Messenia, and Solon the law giver of Athens follow. The fortune of Croesus, the suitors of Agariste, and the Athenians at Marathon close the Greek story in lively, short narratives.
27426-shenanigans-at-sugar-creek:
Paul Hutchens published this Sugar Creek Gang story with Wm. B. Eerdmans in Grand Rapids in 1947. The gang already has its hands full with Big Bob Till, big brother of Little Tom Till, its newest member. A new quick-tempered boy named Shorty Long moves into the neighborhood and starts coming to their school.

Shorty and Bob begin to chum around together, and the gang never knows whether a day will pass without a fight or trouble with their teacher. Matters worsen with a new man teacher, whom nobody likes as well as their pretty lady teacher, and Poetry, the barrel-shaped member, writes a poem about him. It is a warm, old-fashioned boys' adventure.
27670-the-treason-and-death-of-benedict-:
John Jay Chapman wrote this verse drama for performance in a Greek theatre, staging the treason and death of Benedict Arnold in two acts. The first act is set on the Hudson near West Point; the second moves to Arnold's sitting room in England in 1801.

Choruses of waves and clouds, a river-god figure in Father Hudson, and a short vocal intermezzo between the acts give the play its classical frame. Chapman uses that frame to weigh Arnold's betrayal and lonely exile rather than to retell the military facts alone.
28647-texas-week:
Albert Hernhuter's Texas Week opens with district psychiatrist Maxwell Hanstark calling on Mrs. Christopher Nest. She answers in the dress the government ordered for that week: white blouse, green skirt and apron trimmed with white, orange slippers, and blonde hair in a neat bun. Hanstark's appointment runs until the end of the week, and he asks what is wrong with her husband.

Mrs. Nest says he sits all day in the backyard staring at the grass, insisting he stands on top of a cliff. He calls her loco, like the cowboys on television, after a Texas Week of old cowboy pictures watched night after night. Readers get a short satire where fantasy and reality trade places.
29638-the-twins-of-suffering-creek:
Ridgwell Cullum, author of The One-Way Trail and The Watchers of the Plains, wrote The Twins of Suffering Creek, printed in 1912 by George W. Jacobs and Company of Philadelphia. Dedicated to his two little chums, Chris and Ridge, it opens with potter's clay, the harvest of passion, and the awakening of Scipio. Later chapters bring Scipio borrowing a horse, husband and lover, and Sunny Oak protesting and trying his hand.

A picture shows a man breathing hotly to Jessie that she is fine. Cullum writes western romance with strong feeling and frontier color. Readers of classic westerns will find a lively tale of twins, love, and trouble on Suffering Creek.
29668-the-flockmaster-of-poison-creek:
G. W. Ogden published this western in 1921, and it opens with John Mackenzie walking to Poison Creek to ask Tim Sullivan for work. Mackenzie has left school teaching at sixty dollars a month. He reckoned that a man who tends sheep can do better. He takes the road on foot, against the custom of the range, because a herder has no use for a horse.

Swan Carlson, Hertha Carlson, and the men of the sheep country fill the tale. It moves through fights, a sheep killer, wild riders, fever, and a broken pact. Mackenzie must learn the flock, the land, and the code of men who guard both. The book stays close to the work itself: long days, lone nights, and the price of holding ground.
4074-swallow-a-tale-of-the-great-trek:
H. Rider Haggard's tale of the Great Trek opens after meat is cleared away, as Suzanne is sent to bed against her will, eager to hear the men's talk. The narrator seats himself so candlelight leaves his face in shadow and falls full on the three men.

He means to tell lies about the matter at hand, and admits the cunning of his pose. The chapter, called The Sin of Vrouw Botmar, sets a story of Boer farmers, guilt, and vengeance on the South African veld. Readers who enjoy Haggard's adventure romances will find a brisk, old-fashioned tale of the trek.
7893-hide-and-seek:
Wilkie Collins's Hide and Seek, dedicated to Charles Dickens, ranks third among his novels. It first appeared in 1854 at the outbreak of the Crimean War, when readers' minds were fixed on battle news. The first edition sold out to booksellers, then the book went out of print.

Collins refused reprint offers for years, waiting until the novel could appear in a form he trusted. His revised preface explains that wait. The story that follows, of a hidden child, a painter, and a secret past, became a foundation for his later sensation novels, blending domestic life with mystery.
britannica-1911-academy-greek:
Academy, Greek takes its name from a pleasure garden outside Athens, near the river Cephissus, said to have belonged to the hero Academus. Plato had a small estate nearby and taught there for nearly fifty years until his death in 348 B.C. His followers kept the garden as their headquarters until Justinian closed the pagan schools in A.D. 529.

Doctrine changed under each head, or scholarch. Plato's own theory of Ideas was not accepted even by Speusippus and Xenocrates, his first successors. Later heads leaned toward scepticism, doubting that firm knowledge is possible, before Philo and Antiochus blended Academy teaching with Stoic ideas. Cicero, who named his own villa an Academy, represents that final, cautious, eclectic stage.
britannica-1911-bardowiek:
Bardowiek is a village of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hanover, three miles north of Lüneburg on the navigable Ilmenau river. Its population was about 2,000, and its trade rests wholly on farm produce. A Gothic parish church of about 1400 holds remains of a cathedral of vast size.

The past dwarfs the present here. Charlemagne founded Bardowiek in the 8th century and set a bishopric in it. Until Henry the Lion destroyed the place in 1189, it was the most prosperous trading city of north Germany. Its name comes from the Longobardi, the tribe whose home and centre it was, and from whom, the entry says, the colonization of Lombardy started.
britannica-1911-battle-creek:
Battle Creek is a city of Calhoun county, Michigan, in the United States, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands where the Kalamazoo river meets Battle Creek stream, about forty-eight miles south of Grand Rapids. Its people grew fast: 13,197 in 1890, 18,563 in 1900, and 25,267 in the count of 1910. Two railways and electric interurban lines serve it, and the city trades with the rich farm and fruit land around it.

Health food made the city's name. The Battle Creek Sanitarium, set up in 1866, led the way in diet reform, the planned use of food to cure and prevent illness. Its tests grew into the making of cereal health foods, which became the town's chief product. In 1904 Battle Creek ranked first among American cities in food preparations by value. Other goods listed are threshing machines, paper boxes, flour, boilers, and engines. The Grand Trunk railway also kept large locomotive and car shops there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalec-amalek:
The Amalecites, or Amalekites, were traditionally among the fiercest Bedouin tribes. Genesis traces them to Amalec, son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, hence to Abraham, an Arabian origin most modern scholars credit in substance. Nomadic and warlike, their original home lay in the desert south and southwest of Judea, stretching to Egypt's border and Mount Sinai's foot.

Their first meeting with Israel came in the wandering's first year after Egypt, breeding a hatred outlasting their extermination under King Ezechias centuries later. Entering Palestine from the east under Joshua, Israel at first fought other enemies. Saul later opened his reign with vigorous war against the Amalecites, quieting them for many years after a great defeat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-martin-:
Anton Martin Slomsek, bishop of Lavant in Styria, was a Slovenian educator born in 1800. He found Slovenian schools few, weak, and starved of books, as Austrian officials pushed foreign teachers and banned national literature for fear of Pan-Slavism. The constitution of 1848, granting national rights, gave him his opening at last.

With official sanction won after many failed attempts, he reformed the schools, writing many of the new textbooks himself. He founded a weekly paper and backed education rooted in religion and nationality alike. His priests recalled his humility, and the entry honours a bishop who rebuilt a people's schooling against an empire's suspicion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baalbek:
Baalbek, the Heliopolis of Greek and Latin, is a town at the base of the Anti-Lebanon slope. It is now in Lebanon, and the seat of a Maronite and Melchite bishop. Nothing is known of its origin, though guesses link it to Baalgad or Aven. Its monuments include three temples: the Temple of Jupiter, the Temple of the Sun, and the Temple of Venus. Earthquakes and wars have destroyed the town, yet its ruins are called the most beautiful.

The architecture and cyclopean monoliths of the Acropolis draw scientists and travelers alike. Christianity's arrival there is obscure. A doubtful life of St Eudocia names a Bishop Theodotus under Hadrian. Constantine raised a church or turned a temple into a basilica with bishop, priests, and deacons. Under Julian the Christians suffered severely. Orthodox Greeks hold a bishop there, and the British Syrian Schools run a station with a dispensary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-vince:
Vincent Kadlubek, Bishop of Cracow and Poland's early chronicler, reformed a troubled diocese and then retired to a Cistercian monastery. Born at Karnow in 1160 to a wealthy family, he studied to become Master Vincentius by 1189. He was elected bishop after Fulk's death in 1207, and was consecrated in 1208 with Innocent III's approval.

Working with Archbishop Henry of Gniezno, he visited parishes and preached reform. He aided monasteries at Sulejow, Koprzywnica, and Jedrzejow, and helped restore peace between Hungary and Poland over Galicia. Resigning in 1218, he became the first Pole to take the Cistercian habit at Jedrzejow, where he died in 1223. His four-book Chronicle, part dialogue and part personal witness, remains his great work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-week:
Holy Week runs from Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday, kept to commemorate Christ's Passion and the events leading straight to it. In Latin it is hebdomada major, or less often hebdomada sancta, and most modern languages name the stretch from Palm Sunday to Easter Day as Holy Week par excellence. Only German calls it Charwoche, seemingly the week of lamentation.

Whether reverence for these days was primitive is uncertain, though the gospels give a full record from the supper at Bethany through the entry into Jerusalem to the Crucifixion. By the close of the fourth century, reverence certainly flourished at Jerusalem, where the Pilgrimage of Aetheria describes the week's rites in detail. The entry follows Holy Week's antiquity, growth, and ceremonies across the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leopold-janau:
Leopold Janauschek (1827-1898) was a Cistercian scholar, born at Brunn in Moravia. He took the habit at Zwettl in 1846, professed in 1848, and studied at Heiligenkreuz near Vienna, where after ordination he taught history and canon law. His learned work won him Vienna's chair of ecclesiastical history in 1858. His superiors recalled him to Heiligenkreuz in 1859, where he taught until 1877.

During those years he wrote his first great work, Originum Cisterciensium Liber Primus of 1877. It covers the founding, order, and spread of Citeaux, with an account of 742 abbeys of monks founded between the late eleventh and late seventeenth centuries. Its tables show colossal labour of research. A planned second volume on nuns' houses never appeared, though he had gathered much material. His second great work, Bibliographia Bernardina of 1891, the fourth Xenia Bernardina volume, treats St. Bernard's editions and translations, essays on his life, panegyrics, biographers, inscriptions, and historians' views.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-we:
The liturgical week is the seven-day round that shaped early Christian worship, long before feasts filled the year. Jews held the week sacred through Sabbath rest and the Genesis story of creation, and first Christians kept the frame while shifting the chief day.

Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, soon replaced the Sabbath as the great weekly feast. Wednesday marked the betrayal and Friday the Passion, and early writers show Sunday also as a weekly Easter. Later the week kept its weight in the Divine Office, where the Psalter was split across seven days for prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-j-va:
Dominican Theodore van den Broek brought faith to Wisconsin's Indians and settlers. Born at Amsterdam on 5 November 1783, he died at Little Chute, Wisconsin, on 5 November 1851. He learned in Holland, was made priest in Germany in 1809, and joined the Dominicans in 1817. Alkmaar gave him a post in 1819, where he put out sermons for Sundays and feast days.

He reached Baltimore with seven fellow missionaries on 15 August 1832, went on to Cincinnati, and served at Saint Rose in Kentucky and Somerset in Ohio. Green Bay called next, and on 4 July 1834 he found just ten Catholic homes there. He finished Mazzuchelli's church and priest's house, and nursed whites and Indians through cholera with two brave sisters at his side.
far-to-seek:
Diver's Far to Seek is a romance of England and India. Maud Diver also wrote Captain Desmond, V.C. and Lilámani. She dedicates the book to her Blue Bird as an idyll of a mother and son. Lines from Rabindranath Tagore and John Fletcher front the title page.

Her author's note sets part of the tale in Lahore in April 1919. That was the time of the outbreak there, she states. Main events stay true to fact, while all characters are imaginary. Opinions voiced by Indian characters rest on real Indian words, loyal or disaffected. No serious British casualties occurred in her telling, she adds. The note frames a novel written close to raw events. Romance and reportage meet in its pages.
hygromanteia-delatte-1927-greek:
Armand Delatte, a Belgian scholar of Greek magic, printed his Anecdota Atheniensia at Liège in 1927. Pages 397 to 445 hold the Hygromanteia, the Greek Magical Treatise of Solomon. The text is in Greek, copied from old manuscripts held in Athens.

The treatise teaches water divination and the calling of spirits tied to the planets. It lists ranks of angels and demons, and gives prayers and seals for ruling them. Older than the famous Key of Solomon, it stands near the root of the whole Solomonic grimoire line. Delatte's printing kept the work from being lost with its manuscripts.
podcast-dannyjones-L_3_D1b0WEk:
Bart Ehrman is one of the best-known scholars of the New Testament, a former believer whose textual studies led him out of his faith. With Danny Jones, the ancient religion expert discusses the secret gospels, the writings the early church excluded, and his account of where the historical Jesus can and cannot be found.

Ehrman explains how scholars date texts, spot edits, and rebuild what the first Christians actually believed before doctrine settled. Jones asks the questions his audience brings, including the conspiratorial ones, and Ehrman answers them with a teacher's patience and a skeptic's edge. Little here is fringe; the disputes are the real ones inside biblical scholarship. The episode gives listeners the mainstream critical case on Jesus and the gospels, from its most famous living presenter.
swallow-a-tale-of-the-great-trek:
H. Rider Haggard's Swallow, A Tale of the Great Trek, tells a South African story through the mouth of Vrouw Botmar, whose tale the first chapter introduces. Suzanne Botmar finds the shipwrecked Ralph Kenzie, and their love runs through the book's long chain of chapters.

The contents pass through shipwreck, the coming of Englishmen, Suzanne saving the witch-finder Sihamba, a wedding, and Ralph returning into the sea and coming back to the farm. The white swallow gives an omen, and the war of the clean spear, the madness of Ralph, and the Great Trek itself follow. Swart Piet sets a snare, an impi comes, thirst strikes, and the pass of the Quathlamba closes the trek. Haggard mixes romance with the Boer migration's hardships.
the-history-of-caliph-vathek:
William Beckford wrote The History of the Caliph Vathek, shown in the 1887 Cassell & Company edition, with a heading in the record dated 1786. An introduction gives Beckford's family history. Born in 1759, he was the son of an alderman who twice became Lord Mayor of London, and the family wealth came from plantations in Jamaica.

The introduction jokes that Vathek reads like an alderman's dream after a heavy dinner at the Mansion House. Devotion to the senses fills the tale: tables covered thirty times over for a guest, bowls of rock crystal drained without end, and nightmare events that end in a most terrible heartburn. Readers meet the author through his father's feasts and fortune first.
the-secret-of-sarek:
Maurice Leblanc's The Secret of Sarek was translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The Macaulay Company copyrighted this edition in 1920. A foreword recalls the Hergemont scandal of seventeen years before. Few people remember it now, Leblanc warns. His foreword supplies the details in a few lines.

In July 1902, Antoine d'Hergemont walked in the Bois with his daughter Véronique. Four men assaulted him and felled him with a walking-stick blow. Véronique was dragged into a motor-car despite her struggles. Count Alexis Vorski, a young Polish nobleman, had planned the kidnapping. He loved Véronique, and she loved him. Her father had repelled and insulted him more than once. The wedding followed two months later at Nice. D'Hergemont then kidnapped the couple's child and sailed away in a small yacht, the foreword says.
the-unseen-bridegroom-or-wedded-for-a-we:
May Agnes Fleming begins her novel on a wet, windy November afternoon in New York. Sleet lashes the windows while Mrs. Walraven prepares a ball, her first in twenty years, meant to be among the season's most brilliant affairs. All Fifth Avenue is expected at her brownstone palace of velvet carpets and gilded furniture.

Mrs. Ferdinand Walraven herself is rich, arrogant, and ill-tempered, with few rivals on the avenue in any of those qualities. Her only son sits upstairs smoking cigars and staring into the rainy twilight. Fleming's opening sets wealth and gloom side by side, promising a week-long marriage plot, as the subtitle Wedded for a Week announces, inside fashionable society.
